blocks.prompt: Turning On the Night
blocks.text: Long ago, when the sun went down, the whole house went dark. People lit candles. Candles are small and smoky. Then people learned to send electricity through a thin wire. The wire glowed. It made light with no smoke and no flame. The first good bulb was made in 1879. It glowed for about half a day and then went out. Today a bulb can glow for years. Now you can turn on the night with one finger.

blocks.prompt: The Thread That Glows
blocks.text: Every old-style light bulb hides a thread of metal called a filament. It is thinner than a hair, and it is made of tungsten. Tungsten is the metal that takes the most heat before it melts. When you flip the switch, electricity pushes through the filament. The filament fights back, and that fight turns into heat. It climbs to around 4,500 degrees Fahrenheit. Anything that hot glows, the same way an ember in a campfire glows. That glow is your light. There is a problem. If air touched the filament, it would burn away in a blink. So the glass bulb is filled with argon, a gas that will not burn. The filament sits in the argon and glows for months. The filament is longer than it looks. Uncoil the one in an old bulb and it would stretch about six feet. It is coiled, and then the coil is coiled again, so all that wire fits in a space the size of your thumbnail.

blocks.prompt: Five Percent Light, Ninety-Five Percent Heat
blocks.text: Hold your hand near an old light bulb that has been on for a while and you will feel the truth about it. It is a heater that happens to glow. Only about five percent of the electricity going into an incandescent bulb leaves as light. The other ninety-five percent leaves as heat you never asked for. Incandescent means glowing because of heat. The bulb works by making a tungsten filament so hot that it cannot help shining. Push it hotter and the light shifts from orange toward white. The same rule paints a campfire: the red coals are cooler, the white-hot ones are hotter. The story of who invented the bulb is messier than most books admit. Humphry Davy made electric light in 1802, but it was blinding and brief. Joseph Swan in England and Thomas Edison in America both built working bulbs in 1878 and 1879, and they eventually joined forces rather than fight in court. Lewis Latimer, the son of people who had escaped slavery, then figured out how to make carbon filaments that lasted far longer and cost far less. Without Latimer's work, the bulb would have stayed a rich person's toy. Today most bulbs are not bulbs at all. An LED makes light directly from electricity, skipping the heat, and uses about a sixth of the power for the same brightness. The glowing thread is quietly leaving us.

blocks.prompt: The Bulb That Would Not Die
blocks.text: In a fire station in Livermore, California, a light bulb is glowing. It was screwed in around 1901 and, apart from a few power outages and one careful move down the street, it has not been switched off since. It is hand-blown glass with a thick carbon filament, and it puts out about as much light as a nightlight. There is a camera pointed at it so anyone can check that it is still on. Every bulb sold today would be dead a hundred times over. Why? Part of the answer is honest physics. The Livermore bulb runs cool and dim, and a cool filament barely wears out. Run a filament hotter and you get bright white light, but tungsten atoms boil off the wire until it thins and snaps. Bright and long-lasting pull against each other. Manufacturers picked bright. Part of the answer is less honest. In 1924, the biggest bulb makers in the world met in Geneva and formed a group called Phoebus. Bulbs of that era commonly lasted 1,500 to 2,500 hours. Phoebus agreed that 1,000 hours would be the standard, and member companies were fined if their bulbs lasted too long. It worked. Lifespans fell, sales rose, and the cartel held until the Second World War broke it apart. Historians argue about how much was greed and how much was a genuine attempt at brightness standards, but the fines are on record. So the Livermore bulb is not a miracle. It is a reminder. It shows what a bulb could do if nobody needed you to buy another one, and it has been quietly making that argument in a fire station for more than a century.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Tungsten melts at 3,422 degrees Celsius, the highest of any metal
A filament runs near 2,700 degrees Celsius
Roughly 5 percent of the energy leaves as visible light
Argon fill stops the filament from burning up
Blue LEDs won the 2014 Nobel Prize in Physics
Phoebus cartel, 1924: a 1,000 hour cap with fines

blocks.prompt: Five Percent Light: The Bulb, the Blue LED, and What We Chose to Waste
blocks.text: For most of human history, the sun set and work stopped. Fire pushed the dark back a few feet at the cost of smoke, danger, and constant attention. The candle, the oil lamp, and the gas jet were all improvements on fire, and all of them were still fire. The electric light bulb was the first light in history that did not burn anything in the room. Here is what it does instead. Electricity is forced through a filament of tungsten, a metal chosen because it melts at 3,422 degrees Celsius, higher than any other. The filament resists the current, and resistance produces heat. Driven to roughly 2,700 degrees Celsius, the wire begins to radiate visible light, for the same reason that any sufficiently hot object does: heat makes atoms jostle, and jostling atoms throw off light. This is incandescence, and it is an old trick. A campfire ember does it. The sun does it. The trouble with incandescence is that it is nearly all heat. Of the electricity entering a standard incandescent bulb, roughly five percent leaves as visible light. The rest departs as infrared, which is to say as warmth. For a century we lit our homes with small electric heaters and collected the light as a by-product. The engineering around that filament is quietly clever. Oxygen would consume a glowing tungsten wire almost instantly, so the bulb is sealed and filled with argon, an inert gas that refuses to react. The filament itself is coiled, and the coil is coiled again, packing roughly two meters of wire into a space smaller than a fingernail. Even so, tungsten atoms slowly evaporate off the hot wire and settle on the glass, thinning the filament until it breaks. Every incandescent bulb is dying from the moment it is switched on, and it dies faster the brighter you run it. That trade-off is physics. What was done with it was not. In 1924 the world's dominant manufacturers formed the Phoebus cartel and agreed to cap bulb life at 1,000 hours, fining members whose products lasted longer. Bulb lifespans had commonly reached 1,500 to 2,500 hours. They fell. The cartel is the textbook case of planned obsolescence, though historians note the members also had a defensible interest in standardizing brightness. The escape came from a different physics entirely. A light-emitting diode does not heat anything to make light. Electrons cross a junction between two semiconductor layers, drop to a lower energy level, and release the difference as a single particle of light. The energy goes almost straight into photons. Red and green LEDs existed by the 1960s, but white light needs blue, and a workable bright blue LED took until the 1990s, when Isamu Akasaki, Hiroshi Amano, and Shuji Nakamura wrestled gallium nitride into working. The Nobel committee gave them the 2014 physics prize with an unusually blunt justification: the twentieth century was lit by incandescent bulbs, and the twenty-first would be lit by LEDs. So the glowing thread is going out, after roughly 140 years, and almost nobody will mourn it. It was never a very good light. It was simply the first one that let us decide when the day ended.
